title: The Leonid meteor shower is peaking tonight. Here's how to view it. - The Boston Globe
excerpt: The Leonid meteors are some of the fastest, traveling at 44 miles per second.
content:
If you had been awake in some parts of the United States on the morning of Nov. 17, 1966, and looked up at the clear sky, you might have gotten the sense that you were moving through space.

That early morning, with literally thousands of meteors per minute zipping by in a 15-minute window, the sky was ablaze with streaks of light falling from space. This blast of Leonid meteor showers arguably produced one of the best shower displays on record.

The Leonids, which are peaking now, won’t be as intense this year as that meteor storm 60 years ago, but they will still be exciting to see in the night sky.

This year, the astronomical event peaks overnight Monday into early Tuesday this year. The Leonids started at the beginning of November and typically last through the first couple of days of December. The early sunsets and late sunrises right now give us ample opportunity to catch a glimpse.

The Earth itself is passing through this stream of meteors in the tail of a periodic comet known as Tempel-Tuttle, officially known as 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. The comet is named for William Tempel, of Marseille Observatory in France, who discovered this comet 160 years ago on Dec. 19, 1865.

“It is not fresh material from the comet that we see, but debris from earlier returns that happens to be most dense at the same time,” according to the American Meteor Society. “...When the comet returns in 2031 and 2064, there may not be any meteor storms, but there may be several good displays with rates exceeding 100 per hour.”

Whether or not this year’s shower will be a mere flicker or a blaze, it’s often considered an average meteor shower compared to others. Still, the Leonids, one of the fastest meteors at 44 miles per second, are bright and can also be colorful.

Leonids are also known for their fireballs and Earth-grazing meteors, a meteor that skims the top of Earth’s atmosphere at a very shallow angle, according to NASA.

How to view the Leonids

If you do want to check it out, the best time to do so will be after midnight, Monday night. You want to get somewhere dark and just look up. Although the meteors appear to be radiating from the constellation Leo, they will criss-cross the entire night sky.

As with any nighttime observance, it takes as long as 20 minutes for your eyes to adjust to the darkness. Put your cell phone away as well. Your eyes looking at the cell phone and then looking up will not allow the best viewing.

Most years, this particular meteor shower produces 10 to 15 meteors per hour, which means you might have to wait five minutes or so to see one. Pack your patience and warm clothes since it is, after all, November.

Clear night for good visibility?

Of course, the weather also needs to cooperate. Even if there are high clouds, the meteors are shunted by the cloud cover. However, Monday night looks nice and clear.

The moon will be about 40 percent illuminated and might make it hard to see the fainter meteors while it’s above the horizon.

While you’re waiting, you will also be treated to a stargazing side-show. If you missed the chance to check out Mars, Jupiter, and Regulus before sunrise Sunday, you’ll have another chance Monday and Tuesday mornings to check out the astronomical sight. Mars and Jupiter will rise close together in the eastern sky. No telescope needed.

Something to keep in mind: Every year, the Leonids are the warmup for the major Geminids meteor shower, which this year peaks Dec. 13–14. It’s considered one of the most anticipated showers, behind the Perseids in August. Something else nice to look forward to!
